hints: Look at where the sinoatrial node sits in the wall of the right atrium, and think about where its wave of excitation can spread to first.
Remember the job of the atrioventricular node delay, it lets one pair of chambers finish squeezing blood downwards before the other pair starts.
walkthrough:
**Start with the SAN firing**

The SAN is in the right atrium wall. When it fires, the wave of excitation spreads quickly across the muscle of both atria.

That means both atria contract together first. This is atrial systole, pushing blood into the ventricles.

**Add the short delay at the AVN**

The wave cannot pass straight into the ventricles because of non-conducting tissue. It must go via the atrioventricular node, where there is a short delay of about 0.1 s.

This delay is really helpful. It lets the ventricles fill completely before they contract.

**Finish with the ventricles together**

After the delay, the impulse travels down the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue to the base of the ventricles. Both ventricles then contract together from the bottom up.

So the order is simple: both atria, then both ventricles. That is option B.

options.A: If all four chambers squeezed together, the atria could not fill the ventricles first and blood flow would be very inefficient.
options.B: Correct. Excitation spreads over both atria first, then after the AVN delay it spreads to both ventricles, so they contract as two pairs.
options.C: The left and right sides do not take turns. They work together as a pair of atria and then a pair of ventricles.
options.D: Although the SAN is on the right, the wave spreads to both atria almost at once, and the ventricles also contract together, not right side then left side.
